The Standard Test Problems

Source: R/test_problems.R
test_problems.Rd

Returns eight standard test functions of the optimization literature: a quadratic, a curved valley, three difficult polynomials, two functions with several minima, and one with a kink. Each carries its analytic gradient and Hessian, a customary starting point, its known minimizer and two flags describing the difficulty that it poses. They are exported for testing any optimizer, including one outside the package; check_optimizer() runs the whole battery and passes the Hessian to every method, so a method that requires one is checked like the others.

Usage

test_problems(which = NULL)

Arguments

which

A character vector of problem names, or NULL. NULL, the default, returns all eight in the order of the table above; a character vector returns just those, in the order given, so test_problems(c("beale", "sphere")) comes back beale first. A name that is not one of the eight raises an error listing the eight.

Value

A named list with one element per problem, and each element is a list of nine components:

name

character, the same as the element's name.

fn

the objective, a function of a numeric vector of length p returning one number.

gr

its analytic gradient, returning a vector of length p.

hess

its analytic Hessian, returning a p x p matrix. For abs_sum it is the zero matrix, the Hessian wherever it exists.

par

numeric of length p, the customary starting point.

solution

numeric of length p, the minimizer. For himmelblau this is the one of the four nearest the start.

value

numeric, the minimum. Zero for all eight.

multimodal

logical, TRUE for himmelblau and rastrigin.

smooth

logical, FALSE only for abs_sum.

The eight

namepstartwhat it tests
sphere3(1.3, -0.7, 0.8)no difficulty; a method that fails here is defective
rosenbrock2(-1.2, 1)a curved valley, Hessian condition 2508 at the solution
booth2(0, 0)a well-conditioned quadratic written as a sum of squares
beale2(1, 1)a narrow valley, Hessian condition 162
powell4(3, -1, 0, 1)a singular Hessian at the solution
himmelblau2(0, 0)four minima, all of value zero
rastrigin2(0.4, -0.4)121 local minima on the usual box
abs_sum3(0, 0, 0)a kink at the solution itself

The starting points are the customary ones, which for rosenbrock and powell are the difficult points for which those functions were designed. The Hessian of powell at the origin has eigenvalues 202, 20, 0 and 0, so a second-order method has no curvature in two of its four directions and converges linearly where it usually converges quadratically. rastrigin, by contrast, has 121 local minima on the usual box, so the answer depends on the point at which the run began.

The two flags

multimodal marks a surface with more than one local minimum. A local method that reaches a different minimum there is behaving correctly, and comparing its point with solution would report a failure where there is none. check_optimizer() therefore scores every problem on the value reached and labels these two in its note column.

smooth is FALSE only for abs_sum. Its gradient at the solution is exactly zero, because sign(0) is zero, and at every neighboring point the subgradient has max-norm one. A method that tests \(\nabla f\) therefore reaches the solution without being able to certify it, unless an iterate lands exactly on it; the derivative-free and non-smooth methods report a measure of their own instead, tested by crit_stationary().

The gradient floor when every solution has value zero

A line search accepts a step only when the objective decreases by a definite amount, and near a minimum that decrease is about \(\lVert g \rVert^{2} / (2\lambda)\) for a curvature \(\lambda\). Once it falls below the rounding error of the objective, about \(\varepsilon \lvert f \rvert\), the search cannot verify a trial step and rejects every one. The smallest gradient that a run can reach is therefore of order

$$\lVert g \rVert_{\text{floor}} \approx \sqrt{2 \lambda \varepsilon \lvert f(x^{\ast}) \rvert},$$

which grows with the value at the solution and is zero for every problem here. A log-likelihood divided by the number of observations is of order one at its optimum, so an optimizer that reaches 1e-15 on this battery may stop at 1e-8 there. The default of crit_grad() allows for that.

Adding a constant to any of these objectives changes neither the minimizer nor the gradient, and it reproduces the effect: cg() on rosenbrock with crit_grad(1e-14) and maxit = 20000 converges at \(f^{\ast} = 0\), and stops without converging, at a larger gradient, when a constant of \(1\), \(10^{3}\) or \(10^{6}\) is added (see the examples of crit_grad()).

See also

check_optimizer(), which runs the battery and reports the values reached by a method, and crit_stationary() for the rule of the non-smooth methods.

Examples

names(test_problems())
#> [1] "sphere"     "rosenbrock" "booth"      "beale"      "powell"    
#> [6] "himmelblau" "rastrigin"  "abs_sum"   

# The stated solution of every problem has value zero.
P <- test_problems()
stopifnot(all(vapply(P, function(q) q$fn(q$solution), 0) == 0))

# BFGS solves the curved valley from the customary start.
p <- test_problems("rosenbrock")[[1]]
fit <- minimize(bfgs(), p$fn, p$par, gr = p$gr)
all.equal(fit@par, p$solution, tolerance = 1e-6)
#> [1] TRUE

# Powell's difficulty is a singular Hessian at the solution: the quartic
# terms contribute nothing to the curvature at the origin, so two of the
# four eigenvalues are exactly zero (they print with rounding error of
# order 1e-14) and a second-order method has no curvature to read in those
# directions.
H <- matrix(c(2, 20, 0, 0,
              20, 200, 0, 0,
              0, 0, 10, -10,
              0, 0, -10, 10), 4, 4)
eigen(H, only.values = TRUE)$values
#> [1] 202  20   0   0

# abs_sum has a zero gradient at the solution and a subgradient of max-norm
# one at every neighboring point, so a gradient rule cannot certify it.
k <- test_problems("abs_sum")[[1]]
k$gr(k$solution)
#> [1] 0 0 0
k$gr(k$solution + 1e-9)
#> [1] 1 1 1

# A name that is not one of the eight is rejected, and the message lists
# them.
try(test_problems("banana"))
#> Error : There is no test problem named banana. The available problems are sphere, rosenbrock, booth, beale, powell, himmelblau, rastrigin, abs_sum
